chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
title: Great eaters: Chu Berry, Tyree Glenn, Redman, Calloway, Carter and Hawkins
summary: Jackson and Hinton swap stories of big appetites, including Hawkins ordering two dinners from two Detroit restaurants.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: Uh-huh. While we're on that, on the
question of Fats having a big appetite, you know, you were never known for having a small appetite either.
Oh, yes, but not like him.
Yeah, but tell me about some of the great appetites, some of the great -- Butter, I can remember you sitting down when you were young then and preparing a plate and really going at it pretty good.
Tell me about some of the guys you sat down and ate with?

Oh, Chu Berry, he was a monster with the plate. Tyree Glenn. They used to call each other -- Chu Berry used to call Tyree 'Beef Stew' Berry and -- I mean, Tyree would call Chu 'Beef Stew' Berry and then Chu Berry would call Tyree 'Glutton' Glenn.
(Laughter.)
Now, I've sat with some -- and Don Redman, he was another one that was a fantastic eater.
And he was only five feet tall.
And our former boss, you know, was no slouch, you know. Calloway could eat. I saw him eat.
What about Benny Carter?
Oh, Benny Carter was another one, but Benny Carter could cook, too.
Yeah, he was a great cook.
Yes.
I've eaten at his house.
Yeah, Benny Carter could eat, man, and just sit there and laugh and grin and talk to you to keep you from noticing how much he was eating.
Uh-huh.

And one of those kind of things, you know, one of those kind of guys, you know, that would just talk to you and keep you watching maybe, you know, like somebody watching you to see how much he wasn't eating -- how much he was eating. You know, you didn't have to pay any attention to him.

But, then, -- Let me see, did I mention Coleman Hawkins? Now, Coleman Hawkins used to come to Detroit and he would eat at the restaurant on the corner, Smith's, and there was a restaurant around a side street -- I forget the name of it offhand. But, anyway, he would order his chicken here in Smith's, then he'd go around to the other corner and order a steak dinner there, see? Now, by that time he'd come back and the chicken dinner would be ready. And after he'd finished the chicken dinner, he'd go around the corner and by that time that he finished the chicken dinner the steak dinner would be ready. And nobody would -- knew. You know, they wouldn't even know what he was doing. But, you know, I was always watching people.
Watching them. What town was that in?
Detroit.
I see.

Out at Forrest and St. Adwine out there. There was a lot of colored people lived around that district at that time, you know, and a lot of good restaurants out there, because I can tell you about the good restaurants.
